Deuteronomy 1.audience: Moses speaks to "all Israel on this side Jordan" in the land of Moab, in the fortieth year after leaving Egypt (Deuteronomy 1:1–5). Most of his hearers were children when their parents refused to enter the land.

culture.title: Eleven days' journey
culture.text: The route from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea took eleven days. The contrast with forty years in the wilderness is stated at the very start of the book.

culture.title: Judges for every case
culture.text: Judges were told to hear small and great alike and not to fear anyone, "for the judgment is God's." Bribery and favoritism toward the powerful were common problems in ancient courts.

Deuteronomy 2.audience: Moses reminds Israel that the LORD gave land to Edom, Moab, and Ammon too (Deuteronomy 2:5, 9, 19), so Israel was not to fight them. Hearers knew these peoples as their relatives through Esau and Lot.

culture.title: Giants of old
culture.text: The text pauses to note earlier peoples—the Emims, Anakims, Horims, and Zamzummims—who once lived in these lands. Such notes recorded local history for later readers.

culture.title: Buying food and water
culture.text: Travelers passing through another people's land paid for food and water. Water rights were valuable in dry regions.

Deuteronomy 3.audience: Bashan, east of the Sea of Galilee, was famous for its cattle and oaks (Amos 4:1; Isaiah 2:13). Hearers knew it as land given to half the tribe of Manasseh.

culture.title: Og's bed
culture.text: Og's iron bedstead—nine cubits long, about 13½ feet—was displayed in Rabbath of Ammon. Ancient cities kept trophies of famous rulers.

culture.title: Pisgah
culture.text: Pisgah is a ridge in the mountains of Abarim overlooking the Jordan valley and Dead Sea. From its heights, much of Canaan can be seen.

Deuteronomy 4.audience: Moses reminds the people that they themselves stood before the LORD at Horeb (Deuteronomy 4:10), heard the voice, and saw no form. Many of them had been children or young people at Sinai.

culture.title: Forms of gods
culture.text: Neighboring peoples depicted gods as men, women, animals, birds, fish, and heavenly bodies. Egypt's gods often had animal heads, and the sun, moon, and stars were worshipped across Mesopotamia.

culture.title: Teaching children
culture.text: Most people could not read, so faith and history were passed down by parents telling their children.

Deuteronomy 5.audience: Moses repeats the Ten Commandments to the new generation: "The LORD made not this covenant with our fathers, but with us" (Deuteronomy 5:3).

culture.title: Sabbath for servants
culture.text: Here the Sabbath command adds that servants must rest too, and grounds it in Israel's own slavery in Egypt. In the ancient world, slaves rarely had any right to rest.

culture.title: Coveting
culture.text: The final commandment forbids desiring a neighbor's wife, house, field, servants, ox, or donkey—the possessions of a household in a farming village.

Deuteronomy 6.audience: Deuteronomy 6:4–9 became Israel's central confession, the Shema (from its first word, ‘Hear’). Jesus called its command to love God the first and great commandment (Mark 12:29–30).

culture.title: On doorposts and gates
culture.text: Jewish homes later attached a small case containing these words, called a mezuzah, to the doorframe. Inscriptions on gates and doorposts were also used for public notices in the ancient world.

culture.title: Houses and wells already built
culture.text: Israel would receive cities, houses, cisterns, vineyards, and olive groves they had not built. Cisterns cut into rock took enormous labor to make.

Deuteronomy 7.audience: Israel was to enter a land of seven nations "greater and mightier than thou" (Deuteronomy 7:1). Hearers were small in number compared with the peoples of Canaan.

culture.title: Canaanite worship sites
culture.text: Canaanite shrines had altars, standing stones (images), and Asherah poles (groves), often on hilltops. Israel was to destroy them.

culture.title: Treaty marriages
culture.text: Marriages between ruling families sealed alliances between peoples. Solomon's foreign marriages later led him into idolatry (1 Kings 11:1–4).

Deuteronomy 8.audience: Hearers had lived on manna for forty years. Moses describes the land ahead in terms of crops they had never farmed: wheat, barley, vines, figs, pomegranates, olives, and honey (Deuteronomy 8:8).

culture.title: Seven foods of the land
culture.text: These seven foods were the staple produce of Canaan. "Honey" may include date syrup as well as bees' honey.

culture.title: Iron and copper
culture.text: Copper was mined in the Arabah south of the Dead Sea, and iron deposits were found in the region. KJV "brass" usually means copper or bronze.

Deuteronomy 9.audience: Moses tells Israel plainly that they will not receive the land because of their own righteousness (Deuteronomy 9:4–6), and recounts the golden calf to people whose parents had been there.

culture.title: The Anakim
culture.text: The Anakim were known as a tall, strong people, especially around Hebron. A saying went, "Who can stand before the children of Anak!"

culture.title: Grinding the idol to dust
culture.text: Moses burned the calf, ground it to powder, and cast the dust into the brook. Destroying an image completely showed it had no power.

Deuteronomy 10.audience: Israel kept the second set of tablets in the ark, which the Levites carried (Deuteronomy 10:5, 8). The chapter reminds hearers why the Levites had no land.

culture.title: Care for the stranger
culture.text: Strangers—foreigners living in Israel—had no land or family protection. Israel was to love them, "for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt."

culture.title: Circumcision of the heart
culture.text: Moses uses circumcision, Israel's covenant sign, as a picture for an inner commitment. Jeremiah and Paul later use the same image (Jeremiah 4:4; Romans 2:29).

Deuteronomy 11.audience: Most of Moses' hearers had grown up in the wilderness, but some older ones had seen Egypt. He contrasts Egypt's irrigated fields with Canaan, a land that "drinketh water of the rain of heaven" (Deuteronomy 11:11).

culture.title: Watering with the foot
culture.text: In Egypt, farmers irrigated by opening and closing small channels with their feet, or by foot-powered water wheels. Canaan's farms depended on rain.

culture.title: Former and latter rain
culture.text: The early rains in October–November softened the soil for plowing; the latter rains in March–April filled out the grain before harvest.

culture.title: Gerizim and Ebal
culture.text: These two mountains face each other across the valley of Shechem. Blessings and curses were to be proclaimed from them (Joshua 8:33–34).

Deuteronomy 12.audience: Moses looks ahead to life in the land, when Israel would be scattered across many towns. This chapter limits sacrifice to "the place which the LORD your God shall choose" (Deuteronomy 12:5).

culture.title: High places
culture.text: Canaanites worshipped "upon the high mountains, and upon the hills, and under every green tree." Local hilltop shrines remained a problem through the history of the kings (2 Kings 17:10).

culture.title: Meat at home
culture.text: Once settled far from the sanctuary, Israelites could slaughter animals for food at home, as long as they poured out the blood.

Deuteronomy 13.audience: These laws warn against anyone—a prophet, a close family member, or a whole town—who urges worship of other gods. Hearers lived among peoples where many gods were worshipped side by side.

culture.title: Treaty loyalty
culture.text: Ancient vassal treaties required subjects to report anyone, even family, who plotted against the king. Deuteronomy applies the same loyalty to the LORD.

culture.title: Testing prophets
culture.text: Even a prophet whose sign came true was to be rejected if he called people to follow other gods.

Deuteronomy 14.audience: The food laws of Leviticus 11 are repeated here for the generation entering the land. Hearers are also told how to use the tithe in a land where the sanctuary might be far away.

culture.title: Converting the tithe to money
culture.text: If the sanctuary was too far to carry produce, an Israelite could sell the tithe, carry the money, and buy food there to eat in celebration.

culture.title: The third-year tithe
culture.text: Every third year the tithe was stored in the towns for the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow—a form of local relief for the poor.

Deuteronomy 15.audience: Debt was a constant danger for small farmers. Moses commands a release every seventh year and promises that if Israel obeys, "there shall be no poor among you" (Deuteronomy 15:4).

culture.title: Release of debts
culture.text: Ancient Mesopotamian kings sometimes declared releases of debts on special occasions. Israel's law made the release regular, every seventh year.

culture.title: Sending servants away with gifts
culture.text: A Hebrew servant freed after six years was to be given flocks, grain, and wine, so he could start again rather than fall back into debt.

Deuteronomy 16.audience: Israel's three pilgrimage feasts are commanded here at "the place which the LORD shall choose." Hearers in later times traveled to Jerusalem for these feasts, as Jesus' family did (Luke 2:41).

culture.title: Rejoicing with the household
culture.text: Feasts included sons and daughters, servants, Levites, strangers, orphans, and widows. Everyone in the community shared the celebration.

culture.title: No bribes
culture.text: "A gift doth blind the eyes of the wise." Bribery of judges was common in the ancient world, and the prophets later condemned it (Isaiah 1:23).

Deuteronomy 17.audience: Israel had no king when Moses spoke. This chapter anticipates a time when the people would ask for one "like as all the nations that are about me" (Deuteronomy 17:14), as they did in 1 Samuel 8:5.

culture.title: Horses, wives, and gold
culture.text: Ancient kings displayed power through chariot horses, large harems sealing alliances, and treasuries of gold. Israel's king was forbidden to multiply any of these.

culture.title: A copy of the law
culture.text: The king was to write out his own copy of the law and read it all his life. Ancient kings were expected to uphold law, but here the king is placed under it.

Deuteronomy 18.audience: Hearers lived among peoples who sought guidance through divination, omens, and contact with the dead. Moses lists those practices and forbids them all (Deuteronomy 18:10–11).

culture.title: Divination
culture.text: Babylonian diviners read omens in animal livers, the stars, and the flight of birds. Mediums claimed to speak with the dead. All were common across the ancient Near East.

culture.title: Testing a prophet
culture.text: A prophet whose prediction did not come to pass had not spoken from the LORD.

Deuteronomy 19.audience: Moses tells Israel to set aside three cities of refuge in the land west of the Jordan, adding to the three already named east of it (Deuteronomy 4:41–43).

culture.title: An axe-head flying off
culture.text: The law's example of accidental death is an axe-head flying off its handle while two men cut wood—an everyday accident in a farming community.

culture.title: Boundary stones
culture.text: Field boundaries were marked by stones. Moving them secretly stole land from a neighbor, a crime also condemned in Egyptian and Mesopotamian texts.

Deuteronomy 20.audience: These laws of warfare were spoken to a people about to fight for the land. They set out who could be sent home and how distant cities were to be treated.

culture.title: Exemptions from battle
culture.text: A man with a new house, a new vineyard, or a new bride, and anyone afraid, could go home. Gideon later sends home the fearful (Judges 7:3).

culture.title: Sparing fruit trees
culture.text: Besieging armies often cut down orchards for siege works and to ruin a land. Israel was forbidden to cut down fruit trees.

Deuteronomy 21.audience: These laws dealt with situations in village life where elders of the town acted together: an unsolved murder, a disputed inheritance, and a rebellious son.

culture.title: The firstborn's double portion
culture.text: The firstborn received a double share of the inheritance. A father could not give it to a favorite wife's son over the actual firstborn.

culture.title: Hanging on a tree
culture.text: The body of an executed criminal could be hung on a tree but had to be buried the same day. Paul quotes "Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree" (Galatians 3:13).

Deuteronomy 22.audience: These laws shaped everyday life in Israel's villages, from returning a neighbor's stray animal to building a safety rail on a flat roof.

culture.title: Flat roofs
culture.text: Houses had flat roofs used for sleeping, drying produce, and working. A parapet prevented falls.

culture.title: Mixed fabrics and seeds
culture.text: Israel was not to sow two kinds of seed together, plow with an ox and a donkey together, or wear wool and linen woven together.

Deuteronomy 23.audience: This chapter sets out who could join "the congregation of the LORD," naming Israel's neighbors: Ammonites, Moabites, Edomites, and Egyptians (Deuteronomy 23:3–8).

culture.title: Escaped slaves
culture.text: Ancient treaties often required returning escaped slaves to their masters. Israel was told to give an escaped slave refuge and not hand him back.

culture.title: Eating in a neighbor's field
culture.text: A passerby could eat grapes or pluck grain by hand in a neighbor's field but not carry any away. Jesus' disciples did this on a Sabbath (Matthew 12:1).

Deuteronomy 24.audience: These laws protect the most vulnerable in a farming society: a divorced wife, a poor borrower, a hired worker, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow.

culture.title: A bill of divorcement
culture.text: A written certificate of divorce protected a woman by proving she was free to remarry. Jesus discusses this law in Matthew 19:7–8.

culture.title: The millstone
culture.text: Families ground grain daily with a hand mill. Taking a millstone as a pledge for a loan would take away a family's means of making bread.

culture.title: Paying wages daily
culture.text: Day laborers lived from day to day, so their wages had to be paid before sunset.

Deuteronomy 25.audience: These laws cover justice in court, fair treatment of animals, family duties after a brother's death, and honest trade—matters of daily life in Israel's towns.

culture.title: Unmuzzled ox
culture.text: Oxen walked over grain on the threshing floor to separate the kernels. They were to be allowed to eat as they worked. Paul cites this law (1 Corinthians 9:9).

culture.title: The removed sandal
culture.text: A man who refused to marry his brother's widow had his sandal pulled off before the elders—a public sign of giving up his right. A related custom appears in Ruth 4:7–8.

culture.title: Forty stripes
culture.text: Beatings were limited to forty strokes. Paul later received "forty stripes save one" five times (2 Corinthians 11:24).

Deuteronomy 26.audience: Every Israelite farmer would recite these words when bringing the first fruits of the harvest: "A Syrian ready to perish was my father" (Deuteronomy 26:5), retelling the nation's story.

culture.title: Baskets of firstfruits
culture.text: Farmers brought the first ripe produce in baskets to the sanctuary. Offering the first of the harvest acknowledged that the whole harvest came from God.

Deuteronomy 27.audience: This chapter describes a ceremony Israel was to perform after crossing the Jordan, at Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim. Joshua carried it out (Joshua 8:30–35).

culture.title: Plastered stones
culture.text: Large stones coated with plaster could be written on with ink or paint. Writing on plastered walls is known from ancient sites in the region.

culture.title: Responding Amen
culture.text: After each curse the people answered "Amen," meaning ‘so be it’—binding themselves to the covenant aloud.

Deuteronomy 28.audience: Israel's later history—drought, invasion, siege, and exile—was understood by the prophets in light of these curses. Hearers were warned that disobedience would scatter them among the nations (Deuteronomy 28:64).

culture.title: Treaty curses
culture.text: Assyrian vassal treaties contain curses very similar to these, including skies like bronze and ground like iron. Israel's covenant uses language its neighbors would recognize.

culture.title: Siege famine
culture.text: Long sieges brought starvation so severe that people resorted to cannibalism. This happened in Samaria and Jerusalem (2 Kings 6:28–29; Lamentations 4:10).

Deuteronomy 29.audience: The covenant is renewed in the land of Moab with everyone present—leaders, men, women, children, strangers, and servants—and also "with him that is not here with us this day" (Deuteronomy 29:15).

culture.title: Clothes that did not wear out
culture.text: In the wilderness, Israel's clothes and shoes did not wear out for forty years. Cloth and leather normally wore through quickly on desert journeys.

culture.title: Sodom and Gomorrah
culture.text: The land around the Dead Sea, with its salt and sulphur, was a reminder of the destroyed cities of the plain.

Deuteronomy 30.audience: Moses speaks of a future return after exile (Deuteronomy 30:1–5). Later readers in exile in Babylon heard these words as addressed directly to them.

culture.title: Heaven and earth as witnesses
culture.text: Ancient treaties called on gods as witnesses. Israel's covenant calls heaven and earth as witnesses instead.

culture.title: The word is near
culture.text: Moses says the command is "very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart." Paul quotes this in Romans 10:8.

Deuteronomy 31.audience: Moses, now 120 years old (Deuteronomy 31:2), commissions Joshua before all Israel and hands the written law to the priests and elders.

culture.title: Public reading every seven years
culture.text: Every seventh year, at the feast of tabernacles, the law was to be read aloud to the whole people. Ancient treaties also required regular public reading.

culture.title: Deposited beside the ark
culture.text: Treaty documents were kept in temples near the image of the god. The book of the law was placed beside the ark as a witness.

Deuteronomy 32.audience: Moses teaches this song to Israel so that it would testify against them in later generations (Deuteronomy 31:19). It was meant to be memorized and sung.

culture.title: The eagle and its young
culture.text: An eagle stirring up its nest and spreading its wings over its young was a familiar picture to people who watched birds of prey in the mountains.

culture.title: God as Rock
culture.text: In a rugged land, rocks and cliffs were places of refuge. The song calls God "the Rock" several times (Deuteronomy 32:4, 15, 18, 30–31).

Deuteronomy 33.audience: Moses blesses each tribe before his death. Hearers knew their own tribe's place and character in these blessings, as in Jacob's blessings in Genesis 49.

culture.title: Levi and the Urim
culture.text: Levi is given the Thummim and Urim and the duty of teaching the law. The priests were Israel's teachers as well as its sacrificers.

culture.title: Feet dipped in oil
culture.text: Asher's territory in Galilee was rich in olive groves—"let him dip his foot in oil."

Deuteronomy 34.audience: Israel ends the five books of Moses with his death on Mount Nebo. The text says that no one knew his burial place "unto this day" and that no prophet like him had since arisen (Deuteronomy 34:6, 10).

culture.title: Thirty days of mourning
culture.text: Israel mourned Moses for thirty days, as it had mourned Aaron (Numbers 20:29). A thirty-day period of mourning for leaders was customary.

culture.title: The view from Nebo
culture.text: On a clear day, from Mount Nebo one can see the Jordan valley, Jericho, the Dead Sea, and the hills toward Jerusalem.
